name: Alekhine Defense: Exchange Variation
summary: The Exchange Variation of the Alekhine (1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.exd6) is a solid, positional line that sidesteps the sharp Four Pawns.
intro: The Exchange Variation arises after 1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.exd6, when White resolves the central tension rather than grabbing further space. It is one of the calmest and most positional ways to meet the provocative Alekhine Defense, deliberately avoiding the double-edged complications of the Four Pawns Attack. After the recapture 5...cxd6, Black obtains a sound structure with a half-open c-file, while 5...exd6 leads to a more symmetrical setup. In either case White retains a small, comfortable space advantage and easy development, making the Exchange a popular practical choice for those who prefer a steady, low-risk game.
line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 c4 Nb6 exd6 cxd6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The whole point of the Alekhine Defense is to tempt White's pawns forward and then attack the resulting center; the Exchange Variation answers that provocation by keeping things modest and solid. Instead of building the sprawling pawn chain of the Four Pawns Attack, White cashes in the e5-pawn and settles for a small, durable space edge based on pawns on c4 and d4. The knight on b6 slightly restrains White's queenside, but White develops naturally and aims to prove that the extra central space grants a lasting, risk-free pull.

Black's structure after 5...cxd6 features a half-open c-file, which invites active piece play with ...g6, ...Bg7, ...Nc6 and pressure against d4 and c4. The alternative 5...exd6 yields a more symmetrical pawn skeleton and an open e-file, generally leading to quieter, more balanced play. Either way Black relies on piece activity and precise development to neutralize White's spatial edge, and the middlegames tend to be strategically rich but rarely wild, rewarding sound positional understanding over sharp calculation.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 5.exd6, the two recaptures define the character of the game. The text move 5...cxd6 is the more ambitious choice, giving Black the half-open c-file and central flexibility; play often continues with ...g6 and ...Bg7, developing the bishop to its most active diagonal and eyeing the d4-pawn. The quieter 5...exd6 keeps the position symmetrical and solid, and is favored by those content to equalize comfortably.

In the 5...cxd6 lines White typically develops with Nf3, Be2 and O-O, sometimes preparing a later d5 advance or queenside expansion to make use of the space. Black meets this with natural piece deployment and counterpressure against the c4- and d4-pawns. A well-known aggressive setup for White involves an early Nc3 and Be3 with ambitions of a broad pawn front, but the Exchange as a whole is prized precisely because it keeps the play within calm, understandable channels.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Alekhine Defense is named after Alexander Alekhine, the fourth World Champion, who introduced it in serious competition at the Budapest tournament of 1921. Its hypermodern idea of luring White's pawns forward to attack them later was strikingly ahead of its time. The Exchange Variation emerged as a natural, level-headed response for players who prefer not to be provoked into overextension: rather than accept the sprawling but potentially vulnerable center of the Four Pawns Attack, White simply clarifies the position and banks a modest, safe advantage. It has long been a mainstay recommendation for those seeking an easy, reliable way to blunt the Alekhine.
